topic.title: We review a film by its second half
topic.claim: A comedy gets forgiven for a weak first hour, but a weak last hour is never forgiven, because the last hour is what we carry home.
topic.behaviour: Viewers of Udta Teer laughed, called it paisa-vasool, then argued about the second half, the romance and the climax. The argument is what gets posted.
topic.mechanism: We remember how a thing ended and how we felt walking out. Reviews are written in the parking lot, not in the interval.
topic.group: People who watch a film on the first weekend and then argue about it online
topic.moment: You laugh for an hour, then check your phone in the last twenty minutes, and the film is judged right there.

turn.believed: A film is rated on everything it did.
turn.actually: A film is rated on the part you were tired during.

topic.because: Attention drops after the interval, so the climax has to work the hardest with the least goodwill left.
topic.payoff: Test: write your review before the last 30 minutes, then after. See which one you would post.
topic.send_to: The friend who always says 'first half was great, but...'
real_details: Viewers praised the humour and Ayushmann Khurrana; many said the second half dropped and the climax was illogical.
topic.news_peg: Udta Teer audience reaction reported 24 October 2026.
topic.why_now: The film is in theatres and the argument is live.

score.why: A film is rated on the part you were tired during. Everyone has done this, and few have noticed it.

topic.villain: an attention-fatigue effect where tired eyes judge the ending the hardest

ledger.text: Audience attention and goodwill decline after the interval, so a comedy's climax has to work with a more tired, less forgiving audience, which causes the film's eventual verdict/review to be shaped mainly by its last twenty minutes rather than by the full experience.
ledger.sentence: Attention drops after the interval. The climax has to do the most work with the least goodwill left. So the review writes itself around the part where your eyes were tired. The film gets judged on its weakest room, not its best one.

mechanism.actual_mechanism: The post's claim that an audience's end-state dominates the final verdict matches established behavioral science, not contradicts it. Under Kahneman and Fredrickson's peak-end rule and the serial-position recency effect, people retrospectively judge an experience by its most intense moment and its ending rather than by its total or average, so a weak closing stretch is weighted far more heavily in the remembered verdict than the duration of earlier enjoyment. The attention-drop and goodwill framing is an everyday generalization, but the one checkable mechanism (endings disproportionately shape the review) is demonstrably true.

sources.quote: People judge an experience largely based on how they felt at its peak (i.e., its most intense point) and at its end, rather than based on the total sum or average of every moment of the experience.

The recency effect is the tendency to disproportionately remember and be influenced by the most recent information we have encountered... more recent information receives greater weight in forming a judgment than does earlier-presented information.

sources.fact: Social media users broadly agreed Udta Teer's first half was hilarious but were split on the second half, with specific complaints about the romance track and an illogical climax.
sources.excerpt: The first half was so funny that audiences would be clutching their stomachs with laughter. One viewer stated the first half was "far more enjoyable than several recent Bollywood comedies". A viewer noted: "The film went downhill for me after the interval, but not bad". A Reddit user expressed dissatisfaction with the romantic storyline, stating: "The romance plot for one, doesn't land". One commenter acknowledged the ending's logic issues, writing: "average screenplay hinders an otherwise fresh concept...climax illogical but still fun". Another viewer found: "A couple of comedy scenes work, but overall, it's been a snoozefest".

sources.fact: X (Twitter) reactions to Udta Teer praised the concept and comedy but flagged the second half and writing as weaker, while still noting the climax as a highlight.
sources.excerpt: "The comedy is supported by twists, planning & plotting and patriotism." "Comedy that doesn't depend on outdated social media memes!" "dated humour & second-rate writing" "Complete Paisa Vasool Ride Packed with RAW ENERGY, POWER-PACKED Moments" "What a FAMILY ENTERTAINER it is" "intriguing premise undone by dated humour & second-rate writing" "Netizens are seemingly enjoying the performances but questioning the writing" "the initial chunk of the second half could've been sharper" "Initial chunk of second half has a lot of twists but the final twist...are things to look out for!" "a well written climax are the things to look out for!"

sources.fact: Some viewers on X praised Udta Teer's climax as a highlight that rewards attentive viewers, and found the romance track between Ayushmann Khurrana and Sara Ali Khan likeable, contradicting the narrative that the ending is uniformly panned.
sources.excerpt: "The final 20 minutes elevate the film with revelations and twists that reward attentive viewers." "The climax DELIVERS!" and the film features "a knockout climax." "The second half becomes increasingly intriguing, building towards a terrific final act." "Sara Ali Khan looks charming and contributes to the romantic track." "Sara Ali Khan complements him well as Yamini. She adds to the film's light-hearted mood and delivers a likeable performance."

[cover] A comedy is judged on its last twenty [minutes]
The hour you spent laughing never makes it into the review.
 

[slide 1] A comedy is judged on its last twenty minutes.
Swipe to read →

[slide 2] It's Friday night, first show. Four of you, a tub of popcorn already going cold, phones on silent.
The first hour, you're clutching your stomach. Every line lands. You lean over to your friend: paisa vasool, pakka.

[slide 3] Then the interval samosa, and something shifts.
The jokes thin out. The romance track starts wandering. Twenty minutes from the end, your thumb is already lighting up the screen to check the time.

[slide 4] In the parking lot, someone asks how it was. Nobody brings up the hour you spent laughing.
You all argue about the ending that didn't land.

[slide 5] Attention drops after the interval. The climax has to do the most work with the least goodwill left.
So the review writes itself around the part where your eyes were tired. The film gets judged on its weakest room, not its best one.

[slide 6] At the interval your verdict is paisa vasool, pakka. In the parking lot it's 'solid, but that ending though.'
Same film. Only the second verdict ever reaches the group chat.

[end card] Open this again in the parking lot, before you type your verdict in the group chat.
Send to the friend who always says 'first half was great, but...' and never finishes the sentence kindly.

[caption] The first hour buys all the goodwill, and the last twenty minutes spend every rupee of it.
